open-question.question: The draft passes -c (continue the previous session) on one review-milestone-requirements line only. Is session continuation a mechanic the page documents as an axis a reader can combine, or is the flag dropped so every line is a fresh headless run?
open-question.alternative: Remove -c from the two first-review lines so every line on the page is a fresh headless run, and the page mentions session continuation nowhere. Every line then stands on the committed files alone, which is the pipeline's own design: the starting-state pass writes its analysis into ## Relevant starting state as reference material for the passes that follow, and the review pass reads requirements.md whole, so nothing the pipeline persists is lost, each line can name its own host and model with no hidden coupling to the previous line's session, and the flag legend stays at the goal's four flags. It discards the one deliberate carry-over the draft ran (the first review pass starting with the starting-state analysis still in context), and the page says nothing to a reader who wonders whether steps can share a session even though both CLIs offer -c.

Keep -c where the draft has it and present session continuation as a fourth mechanic in the legend: on either host a line carrying -c continues the most recent conversation (Claude Code scopes it to the current directory), so the reader can carry one line's context into the next. It preserves the draft's verified line and hands the reader a lever both CLIs actually offer (claude -c and agy -c), the only way the page can show context carrying over between steps. Continuation sits outside the goal's list of axes (hosts, models, effort) and of kept flags, and unlike those three it does not combine across the host axis: a claude -c line after an agy line continues whatever claude conversation last ran in that directory, silently and without error, so it couples a line to its predecessor's host and to nothing else having run in between, while carrying an already-spent context window into a pass designed to re-read its inputs from the file.

Keep -c on exactly the draft's line, the first review pass after specify-milestone-starting-state, with one in-place sentence saying it carries the starting-state analysis into that review, and leave continuation out of the legend. The closest to milestone 26's word-for-word promotion: the one line the draft verified with the flag ships as it ran, explained once where it appears rather than promoted to an axis. A flag on one line only, tied to one host's session, reads as an unexplained inconsistency (why this review line and not the one in the subsequent-runs way), carries the same most-recent-conversation fragility, and the line is not shipping word for word anyway, since the first-run chains around it are already being rewritten (specify-milestone-starting-state gains its <milestone_id> argument, goto-next-milestone loses its id).
open-question.recommendation: The starting-state pass exists to write its analysis into ## Relevant starting state for the passes that follow and the review pass reads requirements.md whole, so a fresh headless run per line loses nothing the pipeline persists; that self-containment is what lets each line name its own host and model under the Host per line layout, whereas -c is host-local, points at whatever conversation last ran in the directory, and sits outside the goal's lists of kept flags and mixing axes.

Delete the alias lines and the duplicate complete-all-tasks line, so the execute way shows one run of each skill and the page says nothing about usage limits. The page stays strictly about cairn's mechanics: the usage window is a property of the reader's host account and plan that no skill knows about, and no line or sentence then rests on an assumption about how the reader is billed. It takes neither of the goal's two routes for a private alias (placeholder or documented equivalent) and discards the one operational fact the alias encoded, that the heaviest run can stop at a usage limit and is safe to run again because every task commits on its own, leaving a reader who hits the limit to rediscover the resume property.
